text.approach: Access is via Standup Creek Road, reached from Stafford Creek Road off the Teanaway River Road near Cle Elum. The Standup Creek Trail #1369 follows an old road with little early elevation gain, crosses Standup Creek six to seven times, passes through brushy sections with some downed trees, then switchbacks up through forest and meadows to the ~6,200-ft saddle at the head of the drainage. The Labor Mountain Fire closure order on this trail has been lifted, as the Cle Elum Ranger District's trail crew reported on September 25, 2026; expect burned forest and downed trees in the drainage.

text.overview: A quieter, less-traveled alternate approach to Earl Peak's summit from the east via the Standup Creek Trail, which gains a ridge/saddle joining the same upper scramble used by the Southwest Ridge route.
text.descent: Reverse the ridge scramble back to the ~6,200-ft saddle, then descend the Standup Creek Trail back through its creek crossings to the trailhead, or continue over the saddle onto the Bean Creek Trail to exit via Beverly Creek Trailhead if running a loop/shuttle.

text.approach: A roughly two-day approach traveling via the remnants of the McMillan Creek glaciers to reach the base of the peak's north side/northeast buttress; on the day of the climb the party hiked about 3.5 hours from a high camp to the base of the wall.
text.road: {"name":"Goodell Creek Road / Upper Goodell Creek Group Campground trailhead","status":"Open in season; the climb starts on an unmaintained climbers' path, not a maintained trail","driveNote":"Trailhead is the Upper Goodell Creek Group Campground (~600 ft) just off North Cascades Highway (SR 20) near Newhalem. Follow an old logging roadbed about 4 miles (~1 hr) to a cairn/rock-arrow marker (~1,700 ft) where the unsigned Terror Creek climbers' path leaves the roadbed and climbs steeply toward Terror Basin. From the top of the basin a ledge traverse leads north onto the McMillan-Stetattle divide
text.overview: A long, sustained new-wave buttress route up East McMillan Spire's dramatic 2,400-foot northeast wall, climbing compact Skagit gneiss on mostly moderate (5.6-5.8) rock with a handful of 5.9 pitches and three or four pitches of 5.10-.
text.descent: The first-ascent party descended by rappelling back down through the upper north face and the north/northeast buttress system over the course of a day, retracing the general line of ascent to their camp below the wall.

text.approach: From the Lower Goodell Creek trailhead, day one covers more than six miles and 6,000 feet of elevation gain to a col near the Chopping Block. Day two crosses snow, slabs, and talus through Crescent Creek Basin, then crampons up to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, followed by one rappel down onto the Mustard Glacier to reach the base of the North Buttress.

text.approach: From a camp on the Chopping Block ridge, traverse Crescent Creek Basin and climb to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then descend its north side onto the Mustard Glacier; the couloir starts roughly 1,000 ft below the col and tops out at the Eye Col between the two Needles. The usual way down is by the gullies on the south side of the Eye Col back into Crescent Creek Basin.

text.approach: Reach Prusik Pass either from the west (Stuart Lake TH -> Colchuck Lake -> Aasgard Pass -> across the core Enchantment basin) or from the north/east via the longer Snow Creek/Snow Lakes trail (FST 1553) and the upper basin. From Prusik Pass, head west onto Enchantment Peak's east ridge.

text.overview: The most-traveled, standard line up Enchantment Peak: reach Prusik Pass from the core Enchantment basin, then work west along the peak's east ridge over a couple of minor humps to a short, exposed 3rd-class step onto the small, flat true summit block.
text.descent: Downclimb the short 3rd-class step off the summit block carefully, then walk the ridge's minor humps back east to Prusik Pass. From there, descend the same way you came in — either back over Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake, or out via the Snow Lakes trail if approached from that side.
